summary:
Mato Grosso do Sul stands under Brazil's national framework for LGBTI people, and the sources in this inventory identify no state-specific statute, court ruling or enforcement pattern that differentiates the state for a visitor. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013, adopted through National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which binds every civil registry in the country after a 14-1 vote; adoption rights followed in 2015, and lesbian, gay and bisexual people serve openly in the armed forces.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court ruled that discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitutes a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. That ruling supplies the explicit national discrimination protection that had no dedicated statute before it, and it applies on the same terms in Mato Grosso do Sul as in any other state.

Outright International's country overview, updated in 2026, records that the 2019 ruling makes discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity federally criminal, while noting that no specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists and that repeal efforts are active in Congress. The same overview states that the Superior Court of Justice allowed nonbinary people to amend their civil records in 2023, and that intersex people lack specific protections. The framework described here operates uniformly across Brazil's states.
tangentialFactors:
The protective text of Brazilian law and the record of its use are separate questions. The 2019 Supreme Federal Court ruling closed a gap that had left SOGI discrimination without a dedicated statute, but Outright International's 2026 assessment still describes significant violence and discrimination against LGBTIQ people in practice, and records pending repeal efforts in Congress that could alter the statutory basis of protection.

Two gaps sit alongside the broad framework. Intersex people are not covered by specific protections under national law, and the absence of a dedicated federal anti-discrimination statute means enforcement rests on the criminal provisions the Supreme Federal Court read into Lei 7.716/1989 rather than on a purpose-built civil regime. Nonbinary people gained a route to amend civil records through the Superior Court of Justice in 2023, a remedy narrower than the gender-marker rules available to binary trans people.
localsOnly:
Residents of Mato Grosso do Sul hold the same family and status rights as Brazilians elsewhere: same-sex marriage since May 2013 through National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, adoption rights since 2015, and open service in the armed forces for lesbian, gay and bisexual personnel.

Residents bringing discrimination claims rely on the 13 June 2019 Supreme Federal Court ruling, which treats SOGI-based discrimination as a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989 and carries imprisonment and fines. Because no dedicated federal anti-discrimination statute exists, that ruling is the operative instrument, and residents are exposed to the repeal efforts now before Congress. Nonbinary residents have been able to amend civil records since the Superior Court of Justice's 2023 decision; intersex residents have no specific statutory protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Mato Grosso do Sul-specific enforcement data appears in this inventory: the sources supply national law and national-level assessments only, so the frequency of SOGI-based prosecutions, hate-crime reporting or police handling within the state is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the repeal efforts identified by Outright International in 2026 will advance, stall or be withdrawn is unresolved. The scope of protection for intersex people is described in the sources only as an absence of specific provisions; whether general criminal or constitutional provisions have been applied to intersex-based discrimination in practice is not sourced.

The inventory contains no state-level court decisions, no state human-rights commission findings and no data on detention placement for trans people held in Mato Grosso do Sul, so practice under National Council of Justice Resolution 348/2020 in this state is not documented here.
